questions.title: Layer the primitive streak develops in
questions.question: The primitive streak develops in which layer of the embryonic disc?

explanations.A: Correct. The primitive streak forms at the start of the third week as a median, narrow groove with bulging sides, appearing within the epiblast at the caudal end of the bilaminar embryonic disc. It is the first visible sign of gastrulation, and its epiblast cells go on to invaginate through it, giving rise to every layer of the trilaminar disc.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoblast is the other bilaminar-disc layer, but it is displaced rather than converted as gastrulation proceeds -- it does not form the primitive streak, and it contributes no cells to the trilaminar disc's own three layers.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm is one of the products of gastrulation (formed by epiblast cells invaginating through the streak), not the layer the streak itself develops within.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endoderm, likewise, is a product of gastrulation -- invaginating epiblast cells displace and replace the hypoblast to form it -- not the layer the streak develops in.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The notochord is a separate axial structure that forms from epiblast cells migrating cranially through the primitive node, at the streak's cranial end -- it is a product of the streak's activity, not the layer the streak itself forms within.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primitive streak forms within the epiblast, and that every layer of the trilaminar disc traces back to the epiblast.

questions.title: Week gastrulation occurs
questions.question: On what week of intrauterine life does gastrulation occur?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The second week is dominated by implantation and formation of the bilaminar disc (epiblast and hypoblast) -- gastrulation, which converts the disc from bilaminar to trilaminar, has not yet begun.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By the fourth week gastrulation is complete and folding of the embryonic disc is underway -- the fourth week is too late for the process the question is asking about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fifth week is well into organogenesis, long after gastrulation (and the folding that follows it) has finished.
explanations.D: Correct. Gastrulation is the third week's characteristic event. The primitive streak appears at the start of the week, and through it epiblast cells invaginate to form the endoderm, the intraembryonic mesoderm and the notochord, converting the bilaminar disc into the trilaminar one. The chorionic villi also make their first appearance this same week, alongside gastrulation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The first week covers fertilisation through the start of implantation -- far too early for gastrulation, which needs the bilaminar disc (itself a second-week structure) already in place.

questions.learning_objective: State that gastrulation is the characteristic event of the third gestational week.

questions.title: Sources of intraembryonic mesoderm
questions.question: Sources of intraembryonic mesoderm:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the primitive streak is a genuine source of intraembryonic mesoderm, but it is only one of three named sources, not the complete answer this question is looking for.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the primitive node, the streak's own cranial bulge, is likewise a genuine source of mesoderm, but again only one of three.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the notochord itself contributes to the mesoderm-forming process in the median plane, but it too is only one of the three named sources.
explanations.D: Correct. Kasr's own teaching source names the primitive streak, the primitive node and the notochord together as the three sources of intraembryonic mesoderm. Migrating epiblast cells passing through each of these three midline structures give rise to the mesodermal layer. Because each of the three named options is individually a genuine source, 'all of the above' is the complete and correct answer.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Since A, B and C are each individually true (each is a genuine source), 'none of the above' cannot be correct -- the complete answer is that all three are sources.

questions.learning_objective: List the three sources of intraembryonic mesoderm: primitive streak, primitive node and notochord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 81 = d, remark 'Intraembryonic mesoderm develops from all the 3 structures'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-215BD7E9E58872, whose own definition already names all three sources (primitive streak, primitive node, notochord) in these exact terms.

questions.title: Sites where intraembryonic mesoderm is absent
questions.question: Intraembryonic mesoderm is absent in:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- mesoderm is genuinely absent in the median region occupied by the notochord itself (between the primitive node and the oropharyngeal membrane, this region is filled by notochord and neural tube rather than lateral mesoderm), but this is only one of the sites the complete answer covers.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) membrane, where ectoderm and endoderm fuse directly with no mesoderm between them, is a genuine mesoderm-free site, but again only one of several.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the prochordal plate, the precursor region to the oropharyngeal membrane, is likewise mesoderm-free, but only one of several named sites.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- the cloacal membrane, where ectoderm and endoderm fuse at the caudal end, is the mirror-image mesoderm-free site to the oropharyngeal membrane, but again only one of several.
explanations.E: Correct. Intraembryonic mesoderm lies between ectoderm and endoderm everywhere except at three named locations: the oropharyngeal (buccopharyngeal) membrane and the cloacal membrane, where ectoderm and endoderm are fused directly with no mesoderm between them, and the median region between the primitive node and the oropharyngeal membrane (spanning the prochordal plate), which the notochord and neural tube occupy instead. All four listed sites belong to this mesoderm-free set, so 'all of the above' is correct.

questions.learning_objective: List the sites where intraembryonic mesoderm is absent: the oropharyngeal membrane, the cloacal membrane, and the median region occupied by the notochord/prochordal plate.

questions.title: Germ layers of origin for skin
questions.question: Skin develops from:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the complete answer -- surface ectoderm does give the epidermis (and its appendages: hair, nails, glands), but the skin as a whole has a second contributing layer this option leaves out.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endoderm gives the linings of the gut and respiratory tract and the parenchyma of organs such as the liver and pancreas -- it plays no part in forming the skin.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the complete answer -- mesoderm (via the somite's dermatome) does give the dermis, but the skin as a whole has a second contributing layer this option leaves out.
explanations.D: Correct. Skin has two components from two different germ layers: the epidermis, the surface epithelial layer, is ectodermal, while the dermis beneath it, the connective-tissue layer, is mesodermal (from the dermatome, the dorsolateral part of each somite's dermomyotome). Together these two layers, from two different germ layers, make up the skin -- the fact that the individual dermis-from-somites and epidermis-from-ectoderm questions elsewhere in this bank are each testing one half of.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endoderm plays no part in forming the skin -- the second contributing layer is mesoderm (the dermis), not endoderm.

questions.learning_objective: State that skin has a dual origin: epidermis from ectoderm, dermis from mesoderm (the dermatome).

questions.title: Somite differentiation, comprehensive
questions.question: As regards the somites, choose the correct statement:

options.A: Differentiate into myotomes which give rise to muscles of the trunk
options.B: Differentiate into sclerotomes which give rise to vertebrae
options.C: Arise by segmentation of paraxial mesoderm
options.D: Differentiate into dermatomes which give rise to dermis of skin

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true (the myotome, one part of the dermomyotome, does give rise to the skeletal muscles of the trunk), but it is only one of four true statements the complete answer must include.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is also true (the sclerotome, the ventromedial part of each somite, gives rise to the vertebrae via cells migrating to surround the notochord and neural tube), but again only one of four.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is true as well (somites are the transverse segments produced by segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm), but still only one of four.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single best answer -- this statement is likewise true (the dermatome, the other part of the dermomyotome, gives rise to the dermis of the skin), but again only one of four.
explanations.E: Correct. Somites arise by segmentation of the paraxial mesoderm and each one divides into a ventromedial sclerotome (which forms the vertebrae) and a dorsolateral dermomyotome, which itself splits further into a myotome (skeletal muscle of the trunk) and a dermatome (dermis of the skin). All four statements A-D are individually correct descriptions of this one differentiation scheme, so 'all of the above' is the complete answer.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the full somite differentiation scheme: paraxial mesoderm segments into somites, each splitting into sclerotome (vertebrae), myotome (trunk muscle) and dermatome (dermis).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.20, row 104 = e, remark 'All statements are correct'
field_notes.asu: Embryo 3 Q104, the comprehensive version of the individual somite-differentiation facts tested at Q20, Q24, Q47, Q79, Q80 (held as duplicates).

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-5E63C211DEEE00, whose own definition already states this full sclerotome/dermatome/myotome scheme.

questions.title: Day the anterior neuropore closes
questions.question: The anterior neuropore closes on day:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Day 15 is well before the neural tube has even begun forming (neurulation follows gastrulation, itself a third-week event) -- far too early for neuropore closure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 18 is still within the period of neural plate/fold formation, before fusion of the folds into a tube (and the neuropore closure that follows) has progressed this far.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Day 21 is close to the start of neural tube fusion (which begins in the cervical region and spreads toward both ends) -- too early for the cranial neuropore to have sealed.
explanations.D: Correct. Fusion of the neural folds into the neural tube begins in the cervical (middle) region and spreads bidirectionally, cranially and caudally, so the two ends -- the anterior (cranial) and posterior (caudal) neuropores -- are the last parts to close. The anterior neuropore closes on approximately day 25, before the posterior neuropore, which closes a few days later (around day 27-28).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Day 28 is closer to when the posterior (caudal) neuropore closes, not the anterior one -- the anterior neuropore, being cranial to where fusion begins, seals a few days earlier.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior neuropore closes around day 25, before the posterior neuropore.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 18 = d, remark 'Anterior neuropore closes at 25th day'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-4BC4233153C3DC, whose own definition already states the cranial neuropore closes before the caudal one; this row adds the specific day-25 figure this source teaches.

questions.title: What induces the nervous system
questions.question: Which structure induces embryonic development of the nervous system?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The connecting stalk anchors the embryo to the chorion and later becomes part of the umbilical cord -- it plays no inductive role in nervous system development.
explanations.B: Correct. The notochord, once formed along the embryonic midline, induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate -- the first step of neurulation. Without this notochordal induction signal the ectoderm above it would not commit to a neural fate, so the notochord is the structure this question is asking for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hypoblast is displaced during gastrulation and plays no direct inductive role in neural plate formation -- that role belongs to the notochord, itself a product (not the hypoblast) of gastrulation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The primitive streak is the site through which cells invaginate to form the germ layers and the notochord -- it is the source of the inducing structure, but not itself the thing that induces the overlying ectoderm to become neural plate.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The prochordal plate marks the future site of the oropharyngeal membrane, cranial to where the notochord ends -- it is a landmark structure, not the inducer of the neural plate.

questions.learning_objective: State that the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.17, row 41 = b, remark 'Neural tube forms the brain & the spinal cord' (p.19 prose, immediately following the primitive-node discussion)

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-4BC4233153C3DC, whose own definition already states the neural plate is 'induced by' the underlying notochord.

questions.title: Neural plate origin, precisely
questions.question: Neural plate is derived from:

options.E: Ectoderm on the whole dorsal aspect of the embryo

explanations.A: Incorrect. The notochord is not itself the source of the neural plate -- it lies beneath the ectoderm and induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, an inductive role rather than a direct-origin one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mesoderm is not the neural plate's germ layer of origin -- the neural plate is an ectodermal structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endoderm is not the neural plate's germ layer of origin either -- again, the neural plate is ectodermal.
explanations.D: Correct. The neural plate is ectoderm, but not just any ectoderm -- specifically the median strip lying directly over (dorsal to) the notochord. It is induced by the notochord immediately beneath it. This precise positional relationship is what marks out which part of the dorsal ectoderm thickens into the neural plate, and which stays as ordinary surface ectoderm.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The neural plate is not the whole of the dorsal ectoderm -- only the median strip overlying the notochord thickens into neural plate; the ectoderm lateral to it on the dorsal aspect remains surface ectoderm, destined to become epidermis instead.

questions.learning_objective: State precisely that the neural plate is the ectoderm dorsal to (overlying) the notochord, not the whole dorsal ectoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer key p.19, row 83 = d, remark 'Neural plate is derived from ectoderm dorsal to notochord'

questions.author_notes: Sparse overlay onto CON-DEV-4BC4233153C3DC, whose own definition already states the neural plate is the ectoderm overlying the notochord.

questions.title: Origin of the respiratory passage lining
questions.question: The lining of respiratory passages is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surface ectoderm gives the epidermis and its appendages -- not the mucosal lining of the internal respiratory passages.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neural crest gives peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes and the adrenal medulla -- unrelated to the epithelial lining of the respiratory tract.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm contributes the connective tissue, cartilage and smooth muscle of the respiratory tract wall, but not its epithelial lining -- the lining itself is endodermal.
explanations.D: Correct. The respiratory system begins as the laryngotracheal groove, a diverticulum budding from the foregut. Its epithelial lining -- from the larynx down through the trachea and bronchi and into the lung's own airway epithelium -- is therefore endodermal. This matches the general rule that endoderm gives the mucosal linings of the gut-tube-derived systems, respiratory tract included.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neuroectoderm is the ectodermal lineage that forms the nervous system -- it has no role in forming the respiratory epithelium.

questions.learning_objective: State that the respiratory passage lining is endodermal, as part of the general rule that endoderm gives gut-tube-derived epithelial linings.

questions.title: Ectoderm derivatives EXCEPT pancreas
questions.question: All the following are derivatives of ectoderm EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- the anterior pituitary (from Rathke's pouch, an ectodermal outpocketing of the stomodeum) and the posterior pituitary (a neural-tube outgrowth) are both ectodermal, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- the central and peripheral nervous systems are ectodermal derivatives (neural tube and neural crest respectively), so this statement is true.
explanations.C: Correct. The pancreas is endodermal, not ectodermal -- its glandular parenchyma (the exocrine acini and the endocrine islet cells alike) develops from endodermal buds off the foregut, the same rule that gives the liver and thyroid their endodermal parenchyma. This makes the pancreas the one item on this ectoderm-derivative list that does not belong.
explanations.D: Incorrect as an answer -- the adrenal medulla is a neural crest (ectodermal-lineage) derivative, so this statement is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- the enamel of teeth is ectodermal (from the enamel organ, an ectodermal epithelial structure), while the rest of the tooth (dentine, pulp, cementum) is mesenchymal -- so this statement, specifically about enamel, is true.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the pancreas as an endodermal-parenchyma organ among a list of true ectodermal derivatives.

questions.title: Result of lateral folding
questions.question: Lateral folding leads to the formation of an elongated:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Folding compresses the secondary yolk sac into the vitelline duct rather than elongating it -- the yolk sac shrinks with folding, it does not become the elongated structure this question is asking about.
explanations.B: Correct. The flat trilaminar disc folds cephalocaudally, driven by the growing neural tube and somites, and laterally, driven by the expanding amniotic cavity. As it folds, part of the endoderm-lined secondary yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo as an elongated tube. This gut tube is divided along its length into foregut (enclosed by the head fold), midgut (enclosed by the lateral folds) and hindgut (enclosed by the tail fold).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The allantois is a small diverticulum budding into the connecting stalk -- folding does not elongate it into a tube; if anything it is drawn along with the connecting stalk as the umbilical ring forms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The 'spinal tube' (neural tube caudally) forms by fusion of the neural folds during neurulation, a process that runs alongside but is distinct from lateral/cephalocaudal folding of the disc as a whole -- folding is not what elongates the neural tube.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The heart tube forms from the fusion of paired cardiogenic mesoderm as the head fold swings the future heart region ventrally and caudally -- folding repositions it, but 'elongated gut tube' specifically describes the endoderm-derived structure, not the heart tube.

questions.title: Results of folding EXCEPT
questions.question: All the following are results of folding EXCEPT:

options.A: Forebrain is at the cranial end of the embryo
options.B: Hindgut is enclosed within the tail fold
options.C: Foregut is enclosed within the head fold

explanations.A: Incorrect as an answer -- folding does place the forebrain bulge at the cranial end of the now-cylindrical embryo, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect as an answer -- the hindgut genuinely becomes enclosed within the tail fold as folding proceeds, so this statement is true.
explanations.C: Incorrect as an answer -- the foregut is genuinely enclosed within the head fold, so this statement is true.
explanations.D: Correct. Folding reverses the disc's original layout: structures that started relatively cranial (like the septum transversum) end up caudal, and the connecting stalk -- originally at the caudal end of the flat disc -- is drawn around to become more cranial and ventral, not dorsal. Because this statement says the opposite of what actually happens, it is the false one here.
explanations.E: Incorrect as an answer -- the oral (oropharyngeal) membrane genuinely ends up at the most cranial, ventral position after folding (becoming the future mouth opening), so this statement is true.
